The biggest problem with DNA databases is that law enforcement is too stupid to understand the Birthday Problem.
Enlighten me on what the birthday problem is, again?

How many people do you have to have at a party so that there's a 50% chance that two people will have the same birthday?

The answer generally freaks people out - it's 23.

The problem is that we tend to think of it in terms of "If my birthday is January 8th, what are the odds that someone else has the same birthday?" But the Birthday Problem doesn't care which date - just the odds that two people have the same birthdate.

So here's how this relates to DNA:

DNA evidence was developed based on the scenario: "We have a suspect's blood from the crime scene, and we have a suspect. If the DNA test results match, what are the odds that we have the right guy?" This is the "what are the odds someone else has my birthday" type of problem.

But when you have a sample from a crime scene and you just scan a DNA registry for a match, you've shifted to the Birthday Problem formula - "What are the odds that any two people will have a match?" and the percentages drop a LOT. (Note that as DNA sequencing has improved, finding matches is more accurate)

Mind you, finding a match doesn't mean that person didn't do it, but the person shouldn't be treated as a suspect until more information is gathered - the difference between kicking their door in at 2am and running a credit report to see if they were even in the state on the date of the crime...
